summary.title: What TPMs Do and What Software Engineers Can Learn From Them
summary.one_liner: Learn what the Technical Program Manager (TPM) role covers, how it evolved from Microsoft's Program Manager role, how people become TPMs, and how engineers and managers can work with them.
keywords: transition from software engineer to tpm
working with tpms as an engineer
takeaways: TPMs typically own the 'when' and 'who' of delivery, while PMs own 'why' and 'what' and engineering teams own 'how' (per Yixin Zhu).
The TPM role grew from Microsoft's Program Manager role and is more common at fast-growing and large tech companies, often in organizations of 50+ engineers.
Typical TPM work includes multi-team projects, migrations, tech debt efforts, domain delivery (e.g., mobile), and engineering processes.
People become TPMs from varied backgrounds such as finance, testing, software engineering, and project management, often by transitioning internally.
Engineers and EMs get the most from TPMs by onboarding them to the technical context and treating them as partners rather than project managers or Scrum Masters.
summary.summary: This is Part 1 of Gergely Orosz's deep dive into the Technical Program Manager role, drawing on interviews with five TPMs from companies including DoorDash, Uber, Twitter and Tempo. It covers why the role matters, a definition of TPM responsibilities across strategy and execution, design and architecture, and culture, plus examples of projects TPMs own. It also traces the role's history from Microsoft's Program Manager position, describes common career paths into TPM work, and ends with advice from Sophia Vicent on how engineers and engineering managers can work well with TPMs. The article is written as an opinion-and-experience piece based on practitioner quotes rather than a how-to tutorial.
